reviews.text: An all around beautiful and fun game. It runs well and has some wonderful artwork. There is charming and fun story between all the characters and unique second boss for each character. It's absolutely worth picking up and playing.

A lovely little indie gem - under 10USD! The difficulty is highly modular and you might need to impart some 'house rules' to keep things challenging, unless going infinite is your goal - in which case, there's tons of opportunity to work fate in your favor! The flow is solid and the art styles on display are great! I have some QOL-type grievances (keyboard, controller support), but honestly - with the release sale putting it at 7.19USD and my initial vibe being so good... I'll get over them quickly.

Graphite is a roguelike RPG developed by RipRed and published by indie.io that immediately distinguishes itself through a remarkably imaginative premise and visual style. Rather than presenting another conventional fantasy world, the game unfolds within the pages of a child's sketchbook, where hand-drawn heroes, monsters, and landscapes spring to life. This artistic direction does more than create an eye-catching presentation; it reinforces the emotional heart of the adventure. The world is portrayed as a reflection of a young creator's imagination, allowing fantasy and personal storytelling to blend together in a way that feels both original and meaningful. Every environment and character contributes to a setting that celebrates creativity while hinting at deeper themes beneath its playful appearance. The narrative centers on seven unique heroes who believe they are destined to save their world from an impending catastrophe. Guided by a mysterious figure known as The Scribe, they gradually uncover truths that challenge everything they know about their existence. As the story develops, it becomes clear that each character symbolizes a different aspect of the child's emotions and personality, transforming the journey into more than a traditional battle between good and evil. Themes such as grief, courage, hope, insecurity, and self-discovery are woven naturally into the adventure, giving the story an emotional depth that stands apart from many other roguelike RPGs. The concept of fictional heroes unknowingly representing their creator's inner struggles gives every victory and setback greater significance. Combat is built around a strategic timeline system that encourages careful planning instead of simple turn-based exchanges. Every action influences the order of future moves, rewarding players who think several steps ahead rather than relying solely on stronger equipment or higher statistics. One of the game's defining mechanics is the ability to interrupt opponents through well-timed attacks, allowing players to manipulate the flow of battle and create advantageous openings. Combined with a growing collection of skills, abilities, and artifacts, encounters promise to remain engaging throughout multiple playthroughs. The roguelike structure further enhances replayability by introducing randomized events, evolving enemies, and changing combat scenarios that require players to continuously adapt their strategies. Outside of combat, Graphite places a strong emphasis on player choice through interactive story events inspired by illustrated adventure books. Throughout each expedition, players encounter narrative decisions that can influence relationships, unlock hidden opportunities, or alter future encounters. The heroes accompanying the player, the relics collected during the journey, and previous choices all contribute to how these situations unfold. This design ensures that every run feels distinct, encouraging experimentation while rewarding curiosity. Rather than treating storytelling as a break between battles, the game integrates narrative progression directly into the roguelike formula, making exploration and decision-making equally important components of the experience. Graphite also offers considerable flexibility through its progression systems. Artifacts can be combined in countless ways, allowing players to create highly customized builds that dramatically alter how each run plays out. Since enemies are capable of evolving and even acquiring their own advantages, encounters remain unpredictable even after repeated playthroughs. The combination of seven playable heroes, randomized adventures, and diverse character development systems gives the game strong replay value while avoiding the repetitive structure that sometimes affects games within the genre. Every new expedition offers opportunities to discover different strategies, story outcomes, and gameplay combinations. Visually, the game succeeds in making its notebook-inspired concept feel authentic from beginning to end. Pencil sketches, paper textures, and imaginative illustrations create a world that feels handcrafted rather than procedurally assembled. This distinctive presentation perfectly complements the emotional themes of childhood imagination and personal growth, making the visual style an integral part of the storytelling rather than simply an aesthetic choice. It is a memorable identity that helps Graphite establish its own place among modern indie RPGs. Overall, Graphite presents an ambitious blend of emotional storytelling, tactical combat, meaningful player choice, and highly replayable roguelike mechanics. Its willingness to explore mature themes through the lens of childhood imagination gives it a unique personality, while its strategic gameplay systems promise satisfying depth for players who enjoy thoughtful RPG experiences. If the final release successfully delivers on the concepts presented, Graphite has the potential to become one of the more memorable indie role-playing games in recent years. Rating: 8/10

This is a fun example of a roguelike RPG that clearly put effort into each element. It even includes an auto-battle option for those that might feel a bit overwhelmed with combat options, though (as you might expect) they aren't as tactfully-minded as a player would be. I especially like the juxtaposition of the real and fantasy worlds, and how the deeper into the fantasy the scene is, the more detailed the character design becomes. While I might not be that far into the game yet, I can safely say that I consider this purchase worthwhile.

I'm 5 hours in as of writing this review and this game has a ton of great things going on. First of all, the style and feel of the game is excellent. It feels really polished with a unique and compelling aesthetic. Second, the combat system is unique and interesting and forces good strategy and thought. So far the game has been quite easy but I'm going to be ramping the difficulty up on my next run so I'm hoping and assuming it will get challenging. Something that feels unique in this game is how ridiculous the power swings can be, and I mean this in a good way. Like, your characters get so much more powerful over time but so do the monsters. Just before writing this I had saved up enough money to buy a series of 93 artifact draws all at once. I just sat there for 15 minutes easily doubling my teams power in a single turn. There's something almost hilarious and childlike (fitting with the aesthetic) to have power swing moments like this. The enemies too can go from being complete pushovers to all of a sudden they threaten to one shot your characters. I personally like the volatile feel this gives. Also, the character writing/story is quite compelling and perfectly implemented. I'm really looking forward to playing many more runs. Update: I wanted to update my review with some feedback. The difficulty tuning system is very robust. The game basically lets you edit many parameters of how the game works and assigns a difficulty value to every tweak. There's something like 10-20 different things you can change such as how many artifacts to choose from and how hard enemies scale. This system allows you to tune the game to become impossible to win all the way down to comically easy. Also, the heroes are not balanced. I think it's possible that most of them are balanced with each other but the Hunter hero is crazily imbalanced and easily 2-3 times stronger than all other characters with the rogue being 2nd strongest. I beat a Daring difficulty run with the hunter but that difficulty is unplayable with other characters. Here's what feels most bad about this game. You have to tune the difficulty to the hero your playing, not to your skill or understanding of the game. For some reason this really deflated my desire to keep playing, because now I basically have to make the game easy enough to beat with weak characters if I want to beat the game with each character and that is just not compelling to me. I appreciate that this sandbox approach to difficulty and lack of balance amongst characters might not bother some people, and I still think this is a very cool game that deserves to be played, but for me it has led to prematurely being done with the game. Another negative aspect to the game is the Tarot system which is basically drawing events instead of taking fights. It's a really cool idea that it's up to the player to take events vs fights but unfortunately the Tarot system is tuned in such a way where is appears to basically always be a bad idea to take event cards (except for day 1 in which case it's always the best thing to do). Some of them are quite good but some are bad or neutral and this means that on average the rewards from events are just worse than the rewards from fights. The tarot cards offer a little bit of healing but its inconsequential in my experience. It's a really fun idea to gamble with events but in my experience they are simply on average worse than taking regular fights. My suggestions: I think the difficulty system should have presets available as a challenge to the player in addition to the sandbox approach. For players like me that like to feel in a wrestling match with the developers is creates a concrete challenge that I'm being asked to complete rather than just the feeling that I'm setting up my own obstacle course (which carries a lot less motivation for me). I think all the classes besides hunter (and possibly rogue) should be buffed to keep up with those classes strengths. Also, in my time playing the game it seemed like defensive strategies were generally very bad at any heightened difficulty. They only work when the game is easy enough to just kill everything on the first turn. I think all defensive skills could be buffed without affecting overall balance. Third I think drawing a Tarot card should either heal more or perhaps level each characters health points to create a motivation to draw them. Finally, as I said in my original review the storyline to the game is quite compelling and I liked each character. However, the game gives no indication at all that there will be any more story developments once you beat the game with each character. The game definitely hints at interesting themes and meanings of the "Scribe" character who is obviously the kid in whose world we are playing. I can imagine there could be some really compelling stuff fleshed out about him but unfortunately the game gives no hint if you will ever get that by continuing runs. Anyway, thank you devs for a great and thoughtful game. I enjoyed my time with it and I think a lot of your ideas about the timeline combat and leveling skills worked really well. The camping mechanics and each characters unique activities there are great.
